title: Pangrams
directAnswer: Lowercase the sentence, then check whether all 26 letters a–z appear at least once. Drop each letter into a set (or flip a bit in a 26-slot boolean array) and at the end ask: did I collect 26 distinct letters? If yes it's a pangram, otherwise it isn't. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space because the alphabet is fixed at 26.

rules: Normalise case **first** — `A` and `a` are the same letter, so lowercase (or uppercase) before indexing.
Only the **26 letters** count — ignore spaces, digits and punctuation, never index them into the array.
You need **presence**, not frequency — a `boolean[26]` (or a set) is enough; don't waste a full `int[26]` counter.
Answer is a single yes/no: did you collect all 26? Compare the distinct count to 26, or `AND` a full 26-bit mask.
Return early the instant the set hits size 26 if you want, but a single full pass is already O(n).
whenToUse: You must confirm every symbol of a small fixed alphabet (a–z) appears at least once
The universe of possible characters is tiny and known ahead of time
You care about membership ('did it appear?'), not how many times
A 26-slot array or a single 32-bit mask can stand in for a hash set
antiSignals: The alphabet is huge or unknown (full Unicode) → a real hash set, not a fixed array
You need counts, not presence → use an int[] frequency table instead of a boolean[]
You must find the *missing* letters, not just yes/no → still a set, but you report the gaps
Case actually matters ('A' ≠ 'a') → skip the normalisation step
remember.takeaway: When the alphabet is small and fixed, a `boolean[26]` or a 26-bit integer mask replaces a hash set for free — O(1) space and cache-friendly. The same fixed-alphabet trick powers Valid Anagram, Unique Characters, and any 'have I seen every symbol?' check.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that a known 26-letter alphabet means you can swap a hash set for a fixed-size boolean array (or a bitmask) and get O(1) space, and whether you remember to normalise case and skip non-letters.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting to lowercase the input, so 'The quick...' misses letters that only appear capitalised, or indexing spaces/punctuation into the array and reading out of bounds.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer the bitmask version: a single 32-bit int where bit k means 'letter k seen', then check the mask equals (1 << 26) - 1. It's the same idea with one integer instead of an array.

problemStatement:
A **pangram** is a sentence that contains every letter of the English alphabet at least once, regardless of case.

Given a string `s`, determine whether it is a pangram. Return `"pangram"` if it uses all 26 letters a–z, and `"not pangram"` otherwise.

The sentence may contain spaces and is case-insensitive (`A` and `a` count as the same letter).
constraints: s consists of English letters (upper or lower case) and spaces
understanding: Collapse case, then ask one question: across the whole sentence, did each of the 26 letters show up at least once? You never care about how often a letter appears or where — only that none of the 26 is missing. Spaces and any non-letter symbols are noise to be skipped.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the check case-insensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. 'A' and 'a' are the same letter, so normalise to one case before counting.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the string contain digits or punctuation?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The classic prompt is letters and spaces only, but defensively skip anything outside a–z so an unexpected symbol never indexes out of bounds.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return a boolean or a string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: HackerRank wants the literal strings 'pangram' / 'not pangram'. The core computation is a boolean; format the output at the end.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the alphabet be larger than 26 (Unicode)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not here — it's the English alphabet, exactly 26 letters. That fixed size is what lets us use a boolean[26] instead of a hash set.

approaches.name: Per-Letter Rescan (Brute Force)
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to show you can state the literal reading, then point out it rescans the whole sentence 26 times.
hints: The definition is literally 'every letter a–z appears'. How would you check that definition one letter at a time?
For each letter from 'a' to 'z', scan the whole sentence and ask 'does this letter appear anywhere?'
If any of the 26 letters is absent from a full scan, return 'not pangram'. If all 26 survive their scans, it's a pangram.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Twenty-six independent passes over the string, each O(n), gives O(26·n). Only a couple of loop variables are stored → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct translation of the definition: a pangram contains every letter, so check the letters one by one. For each character `c` from `a` to `z`, walk the (lowercased) sentence and see whether `c` shows up anywhere. The moment one letter is missing, you can answer 'not pangram'.

**Why it is obviously correct.** It mirrors the definition word for word. 'Contains every letter' becomes a loop over every letter; 'contains' becomes a scan for that letter. There is no insight to miss, which is exactly why it's a good opener — you prove you understand the requirement before optimising.

**Why we use case-folding once up front.** Because the match is case-insensitive, lowercase the sentence (or compare case-insensitively) so a capital `Q` still satisfies the search for `q`. Skip this and 'Quick brown fox...' fails to find a lowercase `q`.

**Why we don't ship it.** You read the same characters up to 26 times. For `n = 10⁵` that's 2.6 million character comparisons doing redundant work — you re-discover that `e` is present long after you first saw it. A single pass that records each letter the first time it appears collapses all 26 scans into one. Mention this version, state the `O(26·n)` cost, then improve it.
approaches.insight: Each of the 26 scans throws away everything it learned. The fix is to remember which letters you've already seen so you never look for the same letter twice — that single observation turns 26 passes into one.

A single missing letter is enough to disqualify the sentence.

pitfalls: Forgetting to lowercase, so capital-only letters look missing.
Re-scanning the string 26 times instead of recording letters in one pass.
Using indexOf inside the loop and assuming it's O(1) — it's O(n) each call.

approaches.name: Single-Pass Presence Set / boolean[26] (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Phrase it as 'one pass, mark each letter seen, then ask if I collected all 26'.
hints: Instead of asking 26 times 'is this letter present?', flip the question: scan once and record every letter you meet. What small structure remembers 'seen' for a 26-letter alphabet?
Use a boolean[26] (or a hash set). For each character, lowercase it, and if it's a letter set seen[c - 'a'] = true.
At the end count how many slots are true. If the count is 26 it's a pangram; otherwise not. The array is fixed size, so the extra space is O(1).
approaches.complexityReasoning: One left-to-right pass touches each character once → O(n). The presence array has exactly 26 slots no matter how long the input is → O(1) auxiliary space.
approaches.explanation:
Make one pass over the sentence and, for every alphabetic character, mark its slot in a 26-element boolean array. After the pass, the sentence is a pangram exactly when all 26 slots are set.

**The mental shift from the brute force.** The naive version loops over *letters* and scans the *string* each time — 26 scans. Here we loop over the *string* once and let each character tell us which slot to flip. We collect presence information as we go, so by the end one pass has answered all 26 questions simultaneously.

**Why a boolean array and not a counter.** We never care whether `e` appeared three times or thirty — only that it appeared. A `boolean[26]` captures presence in one bit of meaning per letter; an `int[26]` frequency table would store more than we need. Less state means fewer ways to introduce a bug.

**Why `c - 'a'` is the index.** Subtracting the code of `'a'` maps `'a' → 0`, `'b' → 1`, … `'z' → 25`. That arithmetic is the whole reason a fixed array works in place of a hash set: the letter *is* its own index, so lookup and insert are plain `O(1)` array accesses with no hashing.

**Why guarding 'is it a letter?' matters.** Spaces and punctuation have codes outside `a–z`, so `c - 'a'` would land outside `0..25` and either corrupt memory (C-style) or throw (Java) or index wrongly. Skipping non-letters keeps every write inside the 26 valid slots.

**Why counting to 26 is the final answer.** A pangram is defined as 'all 26 present'. Once the pass finishes, summing the `true` slots and comparing to 26 is a direct restatement of the definition. You can even short-circuit and return early the instant the distinct count reaches 26.
approaches.insight: A fixed, tiny alphabet means a hash set is overkill — the letter doubles as its own array index via `c - 'a'`, giving O(1) lookups with zero hashing and O(1) space. Push it one step further and the whole presence array fits in a single 32-bit integer: bit *k* for letter *k*, then check the mask equals `(1 << 26) - 1`.

dryRun.intro: Mark each letter's slot once; at the end count distinct letters. (Tiny input, so it won't reach 26.)

java.explanation: One slot per letter — fixed size, so O(1) space regardless of input length.
Fold case so 'Q' and 'q' map to the same slot.
Guard against non-letters AND only count the FIRST sighting of each letter.
All 26 slots filled is exactly the definition of a pangram.

python.explanation: Fixed 26-slot presence table standing in for a hash set.

python.line: if 'a' <= ch <= 'z' and not seen[ord(ch) - ord('a')]:
python.explanation: Skip spaces/punctuation and only tally each letter the first time it appears.
Increment only on first sighting so distinct tracks unique letters, not occurrences.
Distinct letters reaching 26 means every letter showed up.

edgeCases.behavior: All 26 letters once → distinct = 26 → pangram. Minimal-length pangram.
Only two distinct letters → distinct = 2 → not pangram, regardless of repeats.

edgeCases.input: s = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
edgeCases.behavior: Mixed case and spaces; folding case and skipping spaces still collects all 26 → pangram.

pitfalls: Indexing a space or punctuation into seen[c - 'a'] — out-of-range write/throw; guard with a letter check.
Using an int[26] frequency table when a boolean[26] suffices — extra state, no benefit.
Comparing the distinct count to 26 but forgetting to fold case, so capital-only letters are missed.

commonMistakes: Not lowercasing the input, so letters that appear only in capitals look absent.
Indexing non-letter characters (spaces, punctuation) into the 26-slot array.
Counting frequencies instead of presence, then mis-checking the 'all present' condition.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting case normalisation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you index the raw character, 'Q' maps to a slot outside a–z (or a different region), so the sentence's only 'q' never marks the lowercase slot and a valid pangram reads as 'not pangram'.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Indexing non-letters into the array
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A space has code 32; 32 - 'a' is negative, so seen[c - 'a'] reads/writes out of bounds. Always confirm the character is a–z before computing the index.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for ch in s.lower():
    seen[ord(ch) - ord('a')] = True

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Checking length instead of distinct presence
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Comparing the sentence length to 26 (or counting total characters) confuses occurrences with distinct letters; 'aaaa…' of length 26 is not a pangram.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return "pangram" if len(set(c for c in s.lower() if c.isalpha())) == 26 else "not pangram"

patternNote: Fixed-alphabet presence tracking. When the universe of characters is small and known (26 letters), a boolean[26] or a 26-bit integer mask replaces a hash set: the character is its own index via c - 'a', giving O(1) lookups and O(1) space. The same trick underlies Valid Anagram, unique-character checks, and any 'have I seen every symbol?' question.
